subject: soviet factory workers
title: What If the Weekend Was Abolished? The Soviets Tried for 11 Years

scenes.text: What if the weekend was abolished? The Soviet Union tried it for eleven years.
In 1929, Stalin's planners split every worker into five color groups: yellow, pink, red, purple, green.
Each group worked four days and rested on the fifth, staggered, so factories never stopped. By 1930, 73 percent of industry ran this way.
Output was supposed to jump. Instead machines ran nonstop, broke down and could not be repaired.
And your rest day was almost never your spouse's. Letters to Pravda complained that a day off alone is no holiday.
By 1931 it was a six-day week. In June 1940 Sunday returned, along with a law making 20 minutes' lateness a crime.

description:
What if the weekend was abolished? From 1929 the Soviet Union ran a continuous work week: workers were split into five color-coded groups, each working four days and resting on the fifth, so factories never stopped. Officially 73 percent of industrial workers were on it by October 1930.
Machines running around the clock broke down, and families rarely shared a day off. A six-day week replaced it from 1931, and the seven-day week with Sunday returned on 27 June 1940.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: Each color group had its own symbol on the calendar, so you looked up your day off by color. Which color group would you have wanted, and what should we run through next?
